question: Can the lossless compression rate of a base language model on raw domain text serve as a simple, contamination-resistant predictor of its aggregate benchmark ability in that domain?

key_findings.claim: The paper treats an autoregressive language model as a lossless compressor and measures bits per character on external corpora instead of relying on its tokenizer-dependent perplexity.
key_findings.evidence: Token negative log likelihood is converted to code length and normalized by raw characters, enabling comparison across vocabularies. Sliding windows handle context limits, and corpora are selected for knowledge, code, and mathematics domains.

key_findings.claim: Across 31 public base models, domain-matched bits per character is approximately linearly related to average benchmark performance.
key_findings.evidence: Scatter plots for knowledge/commonsense, coding, and mathematical reasoning show strong Pearson correlations between lower BPC and higher benchmark averages across model families and sizes; mismatched corpora correlate less well.

key_findings.claim: Combining domain corpora can predict composite ability better than a generic corpus alone, and the relationship is relatively stable to resampling and prompt style in the tested controls.
key_findings.evidence: The authors mix Python with arXiv mathematics text for program-aided math and sweep corpus mixture, window, repeat samples, and MMLU input format; correlations remain high in their reported ranges.

key_findings.claim: The linear relationship is observational and can be explained partly by latent scale, data quality, architecture, or training-compute differences shared by compression and benchmark scores.
key_findings.evidence: Models are not trained under controlled interventions, family points are correlated, and benchmark averages are themselves noisy proxies. The paper focuses on public base models with moderate contexts and does not establish that improving a model's BPC causally improves reasoning.

method.core_idea: Use a model's coding length on fresh, raw domain text as a task-agnostic capability measurement and regress benchmark performance against it.
method.mechanism: For each base LM, sliding-window log likelihood produces bits per character on Common Crawl-like knowledge text, Python, and arXiv mathematics. Twelve benchmarks are grouped by domain; correlations and linear fits are computed across 31 models, followed by corpus-mixture, prompt, and resampling checks.
assumptions: Evaluation corpora are sufficiently outside model training data that compression is not dominated by memorization.
Bits per character is comparable across tokenizers and context implementations after the stated normalization.
Grouped benchmark averages represent coherent latent capabilities.
Cross-model correlation is not driven entirely by size, family, compute, or undisclosed training-corpus overlap.

techniques.role: Interprets token log loss as an ideal lossless code length.
Compares compression across different tokenizers on raw text.
Associates knowledge, code, and math text compression with corresponding benchmarks.
Tests whether one compression variable predicts benchmark aggregates.

evaluations.setting: 31 public base language models spanning architectures and scales, evaluated on knowledge/commonsense corpora and benchmarks.
evaluations.metric: Pearson correlation and linear relationship between BPC and average benchmark score.
evaluations.result: Lower BPC strongly tracks higher grouped knowledge and commonsense performance in the reported model panel.
evaluations.baseline: Individual benchmark scores and unmatched compression corpora.

evaluations.setting: Python compression versus coding benchmarks and arXiv-math compression versus mathematics benchmarks.
evaluations.result: Domain-matched compression predicts the respective average more strongly than generic text compression; mixed Python/math text better tracks program-aided math.
evaluations.baseline: Common Crawl BPC and single-domain corpora for composite tasks.

evaluations.setting: Window length, corpus-mixture, repeat-sampling, model-architecture, and MMLU prompt-format controls.
evaluations.metric: Stability of Pearson correlation and rank order.
evaluations.result: The central correlation remains high over the tested choices, though the controls do not remove scale/family confounding.

limitations: Cross-sectional correlation does not demonstrate that compression is a causal or sufficient definition of intelligence.
Unknown pretraining data makes contamination difficult to exclude even with contemporary external corpora.
Only base models are emphasized; instruction tuning, tool use, long-context behavior, and interactive agents can alter ability without comparable raw-text BPC changes.
Averaging heterogeneous benchmarks hides skill-specific deviations and ceiling/floor effects.
Related models from the same family are not statistically independent observations.
failure_modes: A model can compress local text patterns well while failing tasks that require search, tools, or long-horizon verification.
Training-set memorization can improve both corpus likelihood and contaminated benchmark accuracy.
Tokenizer or byte-normalization edge cases can distort apparent cross-model code length.
Domain mixture chosen after viewing results can overfit the benchmark panel.
reusable_insights: Bits per character is a more comparable cross-tokenizer metric than token perplexity.
A cheap unlabeled corpus probe can be a screening metric before expensive benchmark evaluation.
Domain matching and held-out-family validation are essential when interpreting capability correlations.
open_questions: Does within-model intervention—training specifically to improve held-out BPC—cause predicted benchmark gains?
Can compression residuals identify benchmark contamination or unusually specialized models?
How should compression probes incorporate long context, multimodality, retrieval, and interactive decision making?

competitive_landscape.title: Language Modeling Is Compression
competitive_landscape.relationship: Demonstrates that predictive models function as compressors and that large language and multimodal models can compress diverse data types.
competitive_landscape.difference: It emphasizes compression performance and generality; this paper tests whether domain BPC linearly predicts external benchmark ability across models.

competitive_landscape.title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: Establishes power-law relationships between language-model cross entropy, scale, data, and compute.
competitive_landscape.difference: Scaling laws predict held-out language loss from resources; this paper uses normalized loss itself to predict a broad downstream benchmark aggregate across heterogeneous trained models.

competitive_landscape.title: When Benchmarks are Targets: Revealing the Sensitivity of Large Language Model Leaderboards
competitive_landscape.relationship: Examines how benchmark targeting and evaluation choices can make leaderboard conclusions unstable.
competitive_landscape.difference: It critiques benchmark reliability directly; compression-as-intelligence proposes an unlabeled-corpus proxy but still calibrates that proxy against the same kind of aggregate benchmark scores.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: A model's domain-matched lossless compression rate represents its intelligence linearly across knowledge, coding, and mathematics evaluations.
novelty_assessment.evidence: A broad base-model panel shows strong, stable cross-sectional BPC-to-benchmark correlations with domain and mixture controls.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The practical proxy and tokenizer-normalized evaluation are useful; 'represents intelligence' is stronger than the observational evidence, which does not remove scale, family, or contamination confounding.
